def: The state of having more than one possible meaning or being open to multiple interpretations.
ex: There is some ambiguity in the contract regarding payment terms.
nat: Clear documentation reduces ambiguity across distributed teams.

mis.bad: The text has double sense.
mis.good: The text is ambiguous / has some ambiguity.
mis.why: In English, "double sense" is a false friend for "duplo sentido"; use ambiguity or double meaning.

def: Possible to do easily or conveniently.
ex: The architect confirmed that the project is technically feasible.
nat: Given our current budget, this solution seems much more feasible.

mis.bad: This project is very viabilized.
mis.good: This project is very feasible.
mis.why: English does not use "viabilize"; use feasible or viable.

def: Including or dealing with all or nearly all elements or aspects of something.
ex: We conducted a comprehensive review of all company policies.
nat: The onboarding guide gives new hires a comprehensive overview of the product.

mis.bad: He is very comprehensive with my mistakes.
mis.good: He is very understanding of my mistakes.
mis.why: False friend: "comprehensive" means broad/inclusive; "compreensivo" is understanding.

def: A person or thing holding a corresponding position or performing a similar function in another place.
ex: The Brazilian CEO met with her European counterpart in Paris.
nat: I often coordinate features with my counterparts in the design department.

mis.bad: My homologue in the US team agreed.
mis.good: My counterpart in the US team agreed.
mis.why: "Homologue" is rare/technical; in business and professional English, use "counterpart".

def: Showing no activity, growth, or development.
ex: Wages have remained stagnant despite rising inflation.
nat: Without innovation, products quickly become stagnant in competitive markets.

mis.bad: The career became stopped.
mis.good: My career became stagnant.
mis.why: Use "stagnant" to describe lack of economic or career growth.

def: Critical observation or examination.
ex: Public figures face intense scrutiny from the press and social media.
nat: Every line of security code underwent strict scrutiny before release.

mis.bad: The code passed for a big verification.
mis.good: The code came under close scrutiny.
mis.why: "Under scrutiny" is the high-level natural idiom for rigorous inspection.

def: Able to adapt or be adapted to many different functions or activities.
ex: Python is a versatile programming language used for both web dev and data science.
nat: She is a versatile professional who handles both sales and engineering calls.

mis.bad: He is very polivalent in his job.
mis.good: He is very versatile in his job.
mis.why: "Polivalente" translates naturally as "versatile" or "multiskilled", not polivalent.

def: A lack of compatibility or similarity between two or more facts or numbers.
ex: The auditor found a discrepancy between the receipts and bank statements.
nat: There was a noticeable discrepancy between what was promised and what was delivered.

mis.bad: There was a divergence in the accounts.
mis.good: There was a discrepancy in the accounts.
mis.why: When accounting numbers or metrics do not match, use "discrepancy".

def: Strict, precise, and exacting (of regulations, requirements, or conditions).
ex: Aviation security is subject to stringent international regulations.
nat: Our team adheres to stringent data protection policies.

mis.bad: The company has very rigid laws.
mis.good: The company has stringent rules / regulations.
mis.why: For compliance, laws, and professional standards, "stringent" is the idiomatic B2+/C1 adjective.

def: Denoting an action or event preceding or preparing for something fuller or more important.
ex: Preliminary results suggest the vaccine is both safe and effective.
nat: We had a preliminary discussion before presenting the proposal to stakeholders.

mis.bad: We made a preview analysis.
mis.good: We conducted a preliminary analysis.
mis.why: "Preview" is a sneak peek or trailer; for early phases of analysis/results, use "preliminary".

def: Combine a number of things into a single more effective whole, or make something firmer.
ex: The merger helped the tech startup consolidate its market position.
nat: We decided to consolidate all our cloud servers into one unified platform.

mis.bad: We joined all databases in one.
mis.good: We consolidated all databases into one.
mis.why: In professional and tech environments, use "consolidate" for merging disparate systems.

def: Never done or known before.
ex: The tech sector experienced unprecedented growth during the digital boom.
nat: Facing an unprecedented surge in server traffic, our engineers worked around the clock.

mis.bad: It was a thing never seen before in history.
mis.good: It was an unprecedented event.
mis.why: "Unprecedented" is concise, elegant, and native for historic first-time occurrences.

def: Become progressively worse in quality or condition.
ex: Customer relations began to deteriorate after the prolonged service outage.
nat: Without regular updates, software performance will gradually deteriorate.

mis.bad: The situation was getting more bad.
mis.good: The situation was deteriorating / getting worse.
mis.why: "More bad" is grammatically incorrect; use "deteriorate" for formal progressive decline.

def: So delicate or precise as to be difficult to analyze or describe; not obvious.
ex: There is a subtle difference in meaning between these two English words.
nat: Good UI designers pay attention to subtle cues like animations and spacing.

mis.bad: The "b" is pronounced in subtle.
mis.good: Pronounce it /ˈsʌt.əl/ — the "b" is silent!
mis.why: Crucial pronunciation trap: "subtle" is pronounced /SUT-ul/, the "b" is completely silent.

def: Seeming reasonable, probable, or believable.
ex: The engineer offered a plausible explanation for why the database had crashed.
nat: His theory sounds plausible, but we need hard metrics to confirm it.

mis.bad: That makes sense so it is possible true.
mis.good: That explanation is entirely plausible.
mis.why: "Plausible" specifically denotes an explanation or claim that sounds believable and likely.

def: Certain to happen; unavoidable.
ex: With the company expanding so fast, hiring more managers was inevitable.
nat: Change is inevitable in technology; adaptability is what keeps businesses alive.

mis.bad: It was without escape.
mis.good: It was inevitable.
mis.why: Use "inevitable" to express events that could not be prevented or avoided.

def: Producing a great deal of profit.
ex: Cloud consulting has turned into an extremely lucrative industry.
nat: She left her corporate role after landing several lucrative freelance contracts.

mis.bad: It is a very profitable contract (not wrong, but lucrative adds nuance).
mis.good: It is a highly lucrative contract.
mis.why: "Lucrative" emphasizes generating substantial wealth or financial returns.

def: Dealing with things sensibly and realistically in a way that is based on practical rather than theoretical considerations.
ex: Instead of searching for a perfect solution, the tech lead took a pragmatic approach.
nat: Good managers strike a balance between visionary ideals and pragmatic execution.

mis.bad: He is very practical (often misses the nuance of realistic problem-solving).
mis.good: He took a pragmatic stance on the budget cut.
mis.why: "Pragmatic" implies making realistic decisions despite constraints or imperfect conditions.

def: Liable to change rapidly and unpredictably, especially for the worse.
ex: Cryptocurrency markets are notoriously volatile and carry high risk.
nat: In a volatile macroeconomic environment, companies build cash reserves.

mis.bad: The prices are very instable.
mis.good: The prices are highly volatile.
mis.why: "Instable" is incorrect in standard English; use "unstable" or "volatile".

def: Perceptible by touch, or clear and definite; real.
ex: We need to see tangible results before investing additional capital.
nat: Automating customer support delivered tangible cost savings within three months.

mis.bad: We want to see concrete proofs.
mis.good: We want to see tangible evidence / results.
mis.why: In English, evidence is uncountable, and "tangible results" is the standard business collocation.

def: A difficult or unpleasant situation or state of misfortune.
ex: Great leaders inspire confidence and resilience in times of adversity.
nat: Overcoming adversity early in life shaped her entrepreneurial determination.

mis.bad: She suffered many bad lucks.
mis.good: She faced severe adversity.
mis.why: "Luck" is uncountable; use "adversity" or "misfortune" to express serious hardship.

def: A future event or circumstance which is possible but cannot be predicted with certainty.
ex: Every major launch should have a contingency plan in case of outage.
nat: We allocated 10% of the project budget for unexpected contingencies.

mis.bad: We need a emergency plan B.
mis.good: We need a contingency plan.
mis.why: "Contingency plan" is the professional B2/C1 standard term in engineering and management.

def: A typical example or pattern of something; a distinct set of concepts or thought patterns.
ex: Cloud computing triggered a fundamental paradigm shift in enterprise software.
nat: Microservices represent a different architectural paradigm from monolithic apps.

mis.bad: The "g" is sounded: /paradig-m/.
mis.good: Pronounce it /ˈper.ə.daɪm/ — the "g" is silent!
mis.why: Pronunciation trap: "paradigm" rhymes with time/dime; never pronounce the "g".

def: Held or arrived at by the agreement of all people involved.
ex: The board was unanimous in its decision to approve the acquisition.
nat: After an intense debate, the committee reached a unanimous agreement.

mis.bad: The decision was unanimated.
mis.good: The decision was unanimous.
mis.why: False friend: "unanimated" means without life/spirit; "unânime" is unanimous.

def: Becoming more and more rapid (of an increase).
ex: Mobile adoption experienced exponential growth over the past decade.
nat: AI computing power has expanded at an exponential rate in recent years.

mis.bad: The user count grew in exponent.
mis.good: The user count grew exponentially.
mis.why: Use the adverb "exponentially" or the adjective "exponential growth".

def: A thing that motivates or encourages someone to do something.
ex: Annual performance bonuses provide a strong financial incentive for salespeople.
nat: Tax incentives have encouraged many green energy startups to open factories here.

mis.bad: The company gave an incentivization.
mis.good: The company offered an incentive.
mis.why: In English, use the noun "incentive" rather than "incentivization".

pt: concessão mútua, compromisso, escolha entre vantagens
def: A balance achieved between two desirable but incompatible features; a compromise.
ex: In software development, there is often a trade-off between speed and code quality.
nat: Choosing remote work involves a trade-off between flexibility and face-to-face networking.

mis.bad: We have to make a concession between speed and cost.
mis.good: We have to evaluate the trade-off between speed and cost.
mis.why: When choosing between two desirable engineering or life attributes, use "trade-off".

def: A subtle difference in or shade of meaning, expression, or sound.
ex: At an advanced level of English, understanding nuance is vital for diplomatic communication.
nat: Machine translation often misses the cultural nuances of colloquial speech.

mis.bad: The text has delicate tones of sense.
mis.good: The text captures subtle nuances of meaning.
mis.why: "Nuance" is the precise term for subtle shades of meaning or tone.

def: Widespread in a particular area or at a particular time.
ex: Burnout is increasingly prevalent among technology professionals working remote hours.
nat: The belief that multitasking boosts productivity is still prevalent despite research.

mis.bad: This behavior is very predominant in society.
mis.good: This behavior is prevalent in society.
mis.why: "Prevalent" is natural when describing widespread habits, illnesses, or beliefs.

def: Logical and consistent; able to speak clearly and logically.
ex: The candidate presented a coherent strategy for growing the company revenue.
nat: After an all-night coding sprint, he was barely coherent during the morning meeting.

mis.bad: The explanation was without connection.
mis.good: The explanation was not coherent / lacked coherence.
mis.why: Use "coherent" for arguments, texts, or speech that follow clear logic.

def: Based on random choice or personal whim, rather than any reason or system.
ex: Setting a 30-day deadline without assessing the scope seemed completely arbitrary.
nat: The rules felt arbitrary because they were never clearly explained or justified.

mis.bad: He decided by head without reason.
mis.good: His decision seemed completely arbitrary.
mis.why: "Arbitrary" describes actions taken without objective rules or evidence.

def: Extremely thorough, exhaustive, or accurate.
ex: All medical equipment must pass rigorous laboratory testing before public release.
nat: The team applied rigorous benchmarks to test system load and memory usage.

mis.bad: The test was made with big rigor.
mis.good: The test was conducted with rigorous precision.
mis.why: Use the adjective "rigorous testing" or "rigorous analysis" in technical writing.

def: Not certain or fixed; provisional; done without confidence.
ex: We reached a tentative agreement, pending final approval from legal counsel.
nat: Let us set a tentative date for next Thursday and confirm early next week.

mis.bad: We marked an appointment for test.
mis.good: We scheduled a tentative meeting for Thursday.
mis.why: For business dates or agreements that are subject to confirmation, use "tentative".

def: Smooth and effortless; having or creating no impediments or resistance.
ex: Fintech apps aim to make online payments completely frictionless.
nat: Our primary design objective is delivering a frictionless onboarding experience.

mis.bad: The experience had no friction points (not wrong, but frictionless is standard).
mis.good: The user enjoyed a frictionless payment process.
mis.why: "Frictionless" is the dominant B2+/C1 tech and product term for seamless user flows.

def: Innovatively altering or destroying an existing business model or market structure.
ex: Ride-sharing proved to be a highly disruptive technology for urban transportation.
nat: Generative AI represents the most disruptive innovation of this decade.

mis.bad: It disrupted everything so it was disruptor.
mis.good: It was a highly disruptive innovation.
mis.why: Use "disruptive" as the adjective and "disruptor" as the person/company doing the disruption.

def: To distribute resources or duties for a particular purpose.
ex: We need to allocate more budget to security testing this quarter.
nat: The manager allocated three engineers to the migration.

mis.bad: We need to allocate more time for the project.
mis.good: We need to allocate more time to the project.
mis.why: Use "allocate something to" (not for) a task or recipient.

def: To make minor changes to a text, law, or agreement to improve or update it.
ex: The legal team asked us to amend two clauses in the contract.
nat: They amended the policy after receiving customer feedback.

mis.bad: We need to amend about the contract.
mis.good: We need to amend the contract.
mis.why: "Amend" is transitive and takes a direct object without "about".

def: To state a fact or belief confidently and forcefully.
ex: She asserted that the new architecture would cut latency in half.
nat: He had to assert his authority during the heated meeting.

mis.bad: She asserted to us that it was safe.
mis.good: She asserted that it was safe.
mis.why: "Assert" is normally followed directly by a "that" clause without an indirect object.

def: To give someone a particular job, task, or responsibility.
ex: The lead developer assigned the bug ticket to a junior engineer.
nat: Each participant was assigned a mentor for the program.

mis.bad: He assigned me for fixing the bug.
mis.good: He assigned me to fix the bug.
mis.why: Use "assign someone to do something" or "assign a task to someone".

def: To succeed in achieving something after effort.
ex: It took three years of steady practice to attain fluency in English.
nat: Few startups attain profitability in their first year.

mis.bad: I want to attain to B2 level.
mis.good: I want to attain B2 level.
mis.why: "Attain" takes a direct object with no "to".

def: To go around or avoid an obstacle, rule, or standard procedure.
ex: Never bypass authentication checks, even in a staging environment.
nat: We can bypass the city center by taking the ring road.

mis.bad: They bypassed from the approval process.
mis.good: They bypassed the approval process.
mis.why: "Bypass" is transitive and does not take "from".

def: To bring or come to an end.
ex: The legacy API will cease operating at the end of December.
nat: The company ceased trading after the merger.

mis.bad: The noise ceased to making sound.
mis.good: The noise ceased to bother us.
mis.why: Use "cease + -ing" or "cease + to + base verb".

def: To act in accordance with a wish, command, or set of rules.
ex: All vendors must comply with local data privacy regulations.
nat: Failure to comply with the policy will suspend your account.

mis.bad: We must comply the new rules.
mis.good: We must comply with the new rules.
mis.why: Always use the preposition "with" after "comply".

pt: comprometer / ceder para chegar a acordo
def: To settle a dispute by mutual concession, or to expose something to risk.
ex: A weak password can compromise the entire corporate network.
nat: Both sides had to compromise to sign the agreement.

mis.bad: The leak compromised with our reputation.
mis.good: The leak compromised our reputation.
mis.why: When meaning "put at risk", "compromise" takes a direct object.

def: To form or devise a plan or idea in the mind.
ex: It is hard to conceive how the system ran without monitoring for so long.
nat: The founders conceived the idea during a weekend hackathon.

mis.bad: I cannot conceive to live without internet.
mis.good: I cannot conceive of living without internet.
mis.why: Use "conceive of + -ing" or "conceive + noun/how-clause".

def: Giving a lot of information clearly and in a few words.
ex: Keep your status update concise so everyone can read it in thirty seconds.
nat: Her summary was remarkably concise and accurate.

mis.bad: Please write a concise resume with 10 pages.
mis.good: Please write a concise summary in three lines.
mis.why: "Concise" specifically means brief and to the point.

def: To severely restrict the scope, extent, or activity of something.
ex: Tight memory limits constrain how much data we can cache locally.
nat: Budget cuts constrained our ability to hire new staff.

mis.bad: The rules constrained us to do nothing.
mis.good: The rules constrained our options.
mis.why: More naturally used with nouns ("constrain our options") or passive ("feel constrained").

def: To seek information or advice from someone with expertise.
ex: You should consult the security team before opening that port.
nat: I always consult the documentation before changing a config file.

mis.bad: Let me consult with the manual.
mis.good: Let me consult the manual.
mis.why: Use "consult + thing" (manual, doctor) without "with"; "consult with" is for peers/colleagues.

def: To think deeply and at length about something, or to consider doing it.
ex: She is contemplating moving abroad for a senior engineering role.
nat: We briefly contemplated rewriting the entire module from scratch.

mis.bad: I am contemplating to change my job.
mis.good: I am contemplating changing my job.
mis.why: "Contemplate" is followed by -ing, never "to + infinitive".

def: To have a mutual relationship or connection in which one thing affects or depends on another.
ex: High page load times strongly correlate with lower user retention.
nat: Test scores do not always correlate with real-world performance.

mis.bad: Sleep correlates to productivity.
mis.good: Sleep correlates with productivity.
mis.why: Always pair "correlate" with "with", not "to".

def: A detailed analysis and assessment of something, especially a theory or work.
ex: The architect gave a constructive critique of our database schema.
nat: Her critique focused on scalability rather than code style.

mis.bad: He made a critique to my presentation.
mis.good: He gave a critique of my presentation.
mis.why: Use "give/offer a critique of something", not "make a critique to".

def: To reduce in extent or quantity; to impose a restriction on.
ex: Rising cloud costs forced us to curtail non-essential background jobs.
nat: Travel restrictions curtailed international conferences for two years.

mis.bad: We must curtail down the expenses.
mis.good: We must curtail the expenses.
mis.why: Do not add "down" after "curtail"; it already means reduce.

def: To arrive at a fact or conclusion by reasoning from available evidence.
ex: From the stack trace, we can deduce that the token expired mid-request.
nat: Police deduced the suspect had entered through a side window.

mis.bad: I deduced that he left by his empty desk.
mis.good: I deduced from his empty desk that he had left.
mis.why: Use "deduce [something] from [evidence]".

def: To put off an action or event to a later time; to postpone.
ex: Let us defer that architectural decision until we have real traffic data.
nat: The committee decided to defer the vote until next month.

mis.bad: We deferred the meeting for next week.
mis.good: We deferred the meeting until next week.
mis.why: Use "until" or "to" for the new date, not "for".

def: To represent or show something in a picture, story, or diagram.
ex: The diagram depicts how requests flow from the gateway to each microservice.
nat: The documentary depicts daily life in a remote Arctic town.

mis.bad: The chart depicts about monthly sales.
mis.good: The chart depicts monthly sales.
mis.why: "Depict" is transitive and takes no "about".

def: To discourage someone from doing something by instilling doubt or fear of consequences.
ex: Multi-factor authentication helps deter automated credential attacks.
nat: High fees deterred many small businesses from joining the platform.

mis.bad: The price deterred me to buy it.
mis.good: The price deterred me from buying it.
mis.why: Always use "deter someone from + -ing".

def: To depart from an established course, norm, or plan.
ex: Do not deviate from the deployment checklist during a release.
nat: Temperatures rarely deviate much from the seasonal average.

mis.bad: He deviated of the original plan.
mis.good: He deviated from the original plan.
mis.why: Use "deviate from", not "of".

def: To plan or invent a complex procedure, system, or mechanism by careful thought.
ex: We need to devise a faster recovery plan for database outages.
nat: Engineers devised an algorithm that predicts battery wear.

mis.bad: They devised to build a new tool.
mis.good: They devised a way to build a new tool.
mis.why: "Devise" takes a noun object (a plan, a way), not a "to" infinitive.

def: To make or become less in size, importance, or strength.
ex: Repeated delays can diminish user trust in the product.
nat: His enthusiasm did not diminish despite the setbacks.

mis.bad: The risk diminished down over time.
mis.good: The risk diminished over time.
mis.why: Do not add "down" after "diminish".

def: To spread information, knowledge, or ideas widely.
ex: The security team will disseminate the updated guidelines to all offices.
nat: Journals exist to disseminate peer-reviewed research.

mis.bad: They disseminated the news for everyone.
mis.good: They disseminated the news to everyone.
mis.why: Use "disseminate [something] to [people]".

def: To pull or twist out of shape, or give a misleading account of facts.
ex: Outliers can easily distort the average response time in your metrics.
nat: The article distorted his remarks by quoting them out of context.

mis.bad: The microphone distorted with my voice.
mis.good: The microphone distorted my voice.
mis.why: "Distort" is transitive; omit "with".

def: To cause someone or something to change course or turn from one use to another.
ex: During maintenance, we divert all incoming traffic to the backup region.
nat: The flight was diverted to Manchester due to heavy fog.

mis.bad: They diverted the budget for marketing.
mis.good: They diverted the budget to marketing.
mis.why: Use "divert [something] from X to Y".

def: A specified sphere of activity, knowledge, or internet address space.
ex: Natural language processing is a fast-moving domain within AI.
nat: This question falls outside my domain of expertise.

mis.bad: That topic is not of my domain.
mis.good: That topic is outside my domain.
mis.why: Say "outside my domain" or "within my domain".

def: Able to withstand wear, pressure, or damage over a long time.
ex: Invest in durable hardware if the team travels every week.
nat: Stainless steel is far more durable than cheap plastic.

mis.bad: This battery is very durable for years.
mis.good: This battery is durable and lasts for years.
mis.why: "Durable" describes inherent quality, not duration with "for".

def: To develop or present a theory, policy, or system in further detail.
ex: Could you elaborate on why the migration took twice as long?
nat: She promised to elaborate on the proposal during tomorrow's call.

mis.bad: Could you elaborate more about your point?
mis.good: Could you elaborate on your point?
mis.why: Always use "elaborate on [something]", not "about".

def: To evoke or draw out a reaction, answer, or fact from someone.
ex: Open-ended questions help elicit honest feedback from users.
nat: The announcement elicited strong reactions from the community.

mis.bad: The survey elicited for honest opinions.
mis.good: The survey elicited honest opinions.
mis.why: "Elicit" is transitive (no "for"); do not confuse with "illicit" (illegal).

def: To fix an object or piece of code firmly and deeply into a surrounding mass or system.
ex: You can embed the analytics widget directly inside the dashboard.
nat: Security checks should be embedded into every stage of delivery.

mis.bad: We embedded the script inside of the page.
mis.good: We embedded the script in the page.
mis.why: Use "embed [something] in/into [something]".

def: To move out of or away from something and become visible or known.
ex: New AI safety frameworks continue to emerge every few months.
nat: A clear pattern began to emerge once we plotted the errors.

mis.bad: A new problem was emerged yesterday.
mis.good: A new problem emerged yesterday.
mis.why: "Emerge" is intransitive; never use it in the passive ("was emerged").

def: Based on, concerned with, or verifiable by observation or experience rather than theory alone.
ex: We need empirical evidence before rolling out this change to all users.
nat: The study provides strong empirical support for spaced repetition.

mis.bad: That is just an empirical guess without proof.
mis.good: That is a theoretical guess without empirical proof.
mis.why: "Empirical" means backed by real observation/data, the opposite of a guess.

def: To declare one's public approval or support of someone or something.
ex: The security board refused to endorse the unencrypted protocol.
nat: Several industry leaders endorsed the open-source standard.

mis.bad: The team endorsed with the new policy.
mis.good: The team endorsed the new policy.
mis.why: "Endorse" takes a direct object with no "with".

def: To compel observance of or compliance with a law, rule, or obligation.
ex: The gateway will automatically enforce rate limits on public endpoints.
nat: Rules are useless if nobody enforces them consistently.

mis.bad: We need to reinforce the password rules.
mis.good: We need to enforce the password rules.
mis.why: "Reinforce" means strengthen; "enforce" means make sure a rule is obeyed.

def: To involve something as a necessary or inevitable part or consequence.
ex: Migrating to a new cloud provider will entail weeks of regression testing.
nat: What does the senior architect role actually entail?

mis.bad: This job entails to travel frequently.
mis.good: This job entails traveling frequently.
mis.why: "Entail" takes a noun or -ing form, not "to + infinitive".

def: Not even or regular in pattern or movement; unpredictable.
ex: Users complained about erratic network speeds throughout the afternoon.
nat: His sleep schedule became erratic during the product launch.

mis.bad: The server had an errant response time.
mis.good: The server had erratic response times.
mis.why: "Errant" means straying/misbehaving; "erratic" means irregular/unpredictable.

def: To escape or avoid something, especially by cleverness or trickery.
ex: Attackers tried to evade detection by splitting the payload across requests.
nat: He skillfully evaded every direct question during the interview.

mis.bad: The malware evaded from the antivirus.
mis.good: The malware evaded the antivirus.
mis.why: "Evade" is transitive; do not use "from".

def: To make a problem, bad situation, or negative feeling worse.
ex: Running heavy batch jobs at noon will only exacerbate the database bottleneck.
nat: Lack of sleep often exacerbates stress at work.

mis.bad: The delay exacerbated more the conflict.
mis.good: The delay exacerbated the conflict even further.
mis.why: "Exacerbate" already means make worse; never pair it with "more".

def: Stated clearly and in detail, leaving no room for confusion or doubt.
ex: The API requires explicit user consent before accessing location data.
nat: She gave explicit instructions on how to rotate the keys.

mis.bad: He was explicit with his expectations.
mis.good: He was explicit about his expectations.
mis.why: Use "explicit about [something]".

def: To omit or decline to take something pleasant or valuable; to go without.
ex: The startup decided to forgo short-term profits to invest in reliability.
nat: I had to forgo lunch to finish the incident report on time.

mis.bad: I decided to forgo from the bonus.
mis.good: I decided to forgo the bonus.
mis.why: "Forgo" is transitive and takes no "from".

def: Conflict or resistance that slows down a process or interaction.
ex: Removing extra form fields reduced signup friction by thirty percent.
nat: Poor handoffs create unnecessary friction between product and QA.

mis.bad: There are many frictions in the checkout.
mis.good: There is a lot of friction in the checkout.
mis.why: "Friction" is uncountable in English.

def: To estimate or determine the magnitude, amount, or volume of something.
ex: We ran a quick survey to gauge customer satisfaction after the redesign.
nat: It is hard to gauge how long a legacy refactor will take.

mis.bad: Let us gauge about user feedback.
mis.good: Let us gauge user feedback.
mis.why: "Gauge" is transitive (no "about"); note the spelling "-au-".

def: Characterized by a high level of detail or small, distinct components.
ex: Role-based access gives us granular control over who can export reports.
nat: The new dashboard offers a much more granular view of daily traffic.

mis.bad: We need a granularly control of permissions.
mis.good: We need granular control over permissions.
mis.why: Use the adjective "granular" before a noun, not the adverb.

def: To control and make use of a resource or force to produce power or results.
ex: Modern teams harness automation to eliminate repetitive manual checks.
nat: Coastal regions can harness wind energy all year round.

mis.bad: We should harness with AI tools.
mis.good: We should harness AI tools.
mis.why: "Harness" takes a direct object without "with".

def: To create difficulties for someone or something, resulting in delay or obstruction.
ex: Outdated tooling can severely hinder a team's ability to ship safely.
nat: Heavy snow hindered rescue efforts overnight.

mis.bad: Slow tests hinder us to deploy fast.
mis.good: Slow tests hinder us from deploying fast.
mis.why: Use "hinder [someone/something] from + -ing", or "hinder [noun]".
